articles.label: County Budget
articles.headline: Escambia County faces $12 million shortfall as property insurance costs surge
articles.dek: The county's self-insurance fund is bleeding money. Commissioners must decide by month's end whether to cut services or raise the millage rate.
brief: Escambia County's self-insurance fund faces a $12 million deficit driven by soaring reinsurance premiums and a string of severe weather claims since 2024.
County commissioners must choose between service cuts, a millage rate increase, or a combination of both before the fiscal year budget deadline on June 30.
The crisis mirrors statewide trends as Florida's property insurance market continues its spiral, with some coastal counties seeing premium increases of 40% or more.
articles.body:
The fluorescent lights in the Escambia County Administrative Complex hummed over a half-empty meeting room Tuesday morning. County Administrator Wes Moreno stood at the podium with a single slide projected behind him: a red bar graph showing the self-insurance fund's balance cratering from $18 million in 2023 to a projected negative $4.2 million by October.

"We're not here to sugarcoat this," Moreno told the five commissioners seated before him. "We have a $12 million hole. We have 26 days to figure out how to fill it."

The county's self-insurance fund covers property damage to government buildings, vehicles and infrastructure. For two decades, it operated with comfortable reserves built through modest annual contributions and relatively calm hurricane seasons. That changed in 2024.

Hurricane seasons in 2024 and 2025 brought four named storms within 150 miles of Pensacola. While none made direct landfall, the cumulative damage—roof repairs to the county jail, flooding at three fire stations, a collapsed storage facility on Fairfield Drive—drained $9.3 million from the fund in 18 months.

Then came the reinsurance bill.

The reinsurance squeeze

Escambia County, like most Florida local governments, purchases reinsurance to protect against catastrophic losses. The county's policy, held through a consortium of carriers, renewed in April. The new premium: $8.4 million annually, up from $5.1 million the previous year. A 65% increase.

"The reinsurance market has essentially repriced all of coastal Florida," said Risk Management Director Tonya Hitchens during Tuesday's workshop. "We shopped this extensively. This was the best rate we could find."

The county's options for coverage were limited. Two carriers declined to quote Escambia County altogether, citing the concentration of coastal properties. A third offered coverage with a $15 million deductible—triple the current threshold—at nearly the same premium.

Commissioner Jeff Bergosh, whose district includes much of the county's unincorporated coastal areas, pressed Hitchens on whether the county had explored the state-backed Citizens Property Insurance Corporation as an alternative.

"Citizens doesn't write policies for local governments," Hitchens replied. "We're on our own here."

The math

The $12 million shortfall breaks down roughly as follows: $3.3 million in unexpected reinsurance costs above what was budgeted, $4.2 million in pending claims from May's flooding event, and $4.5 million needed to rebuild the fund's reserve to the minimum actuarially recommended level.

County budget staff presented three scenarios Tuesday, each with its own political cost.

Option one: a 0.4 mill increase to the county's property tax rate. For the owner of a $250,000 home with a $50,000 homestead exemption, that translates to roughly $80 more per year. The increase would generate approximately $9.2 million in new revenue, with the remaining gap covered by drawing down general fund reserves.

Option two: $12 million in service cuts spread across departments. Budget Director Amy Rhodes outlined what that would look like—likely elimination of 40 to 60 positions, closure of one or more library branches, reduced hours at recreation centers, and deferred maintenance on county roads. "These are not hypotheticals," Rhodes said. "These are the places the money exists."

Option three: a smaller millage increase of 0.2 mills combined with $6 million in cuts. The hybrid approach.

No commissioner endorsed any option Tuesday. The workshop was informational only, with formal action scheduled for June 18.

Political fault lines

The discussion exposed familiar divisions on the five-member board.

Commissioner Bergosh, who has opposed tax increases throughout his tenure, questioned whether the shortfall reflected genuine need or administrative overspending. "I want to see a line-item audit of every claim paid out of this fund in the last three years," he said. "Before we ask taxpayers for more money, I want to know where the money went."

Commissioner Lumon May, whose District 3 includes some of the county's lowest-income census tracts, pushed back. "We can audit all we want. The reinsurance bill is what it is. Our people can't afford to lose library branches. They can't afford to lose bus routes."

Commission Chair Robert Bender, who faces reelection in November, said little during the two-hour workshop. In a brief interview afterward, he acknowledged the difficulty of the vote ahead.

"Nobody wants to raise taxes. Nobody wants to cut services. But we can't print money," Bender said. "Something has to give."

A statewide problem

Escambia County's insurance crisis is not unique. Across Florida, local governments are grappling with the same reinsurance market that has pushed private homeowners' premiums to the highest in the nation.

Bay County, still rebuilding from Hurricane Michael, saw its reinsurance costs rise 72% this year. Monroe County, which includes the Florida Keys, is considering a dedicated insurance millage for the first time. In Brevard County, commissioners voted in April to self-insure entirely for the coming year—a gamble that would leave taxpayers fully exposed if a major storm hits.

Florida's insurance market has shed carriers steadily since 2020. Citizens, the state insurer of last resort, now holds more policies than at any point in its history. But local governments don't have access to that backstop.

"Municipalities and counties are in a different risk pool," said Robert Hunter, a former Texas insurance commissioner who now directs insurance research at the Consumer Federation of America. "The private market sees them as concentrated risk. One hurricane can wipe out a county's entire property portfolio in a single night."

Hunter said he expects more Florida counties to face similar shortfalls in the coming budget cycles, particularly those with significant coastal exposure.

What happens next

Escambia County commissioners will hold a public hearing on the budget options June 18 at 5:30 p.m. at the County Administrative Complex on Palafox Street. A final budget vote is required by June 30, the end of the state-mandated budget calendar for non-charter counties.

If commissioners fail to reach agreement, state law allows the previous year's millage rate to roll forward automatically—but that would leave the insurance fund shortfall unaddressed, potentially forcing mid-year cuts or emergency borrowing.

Moreno, the county administrator, said staff would provide updated financial projections at the June 18 hearing, including any new claims from the current Atlantic hurricane season, which began June 1.

"We're operating without margin right now," Moreno said. "One bad storm and we're not talking about a shortfall anymore. We're talking about insolvency."

The room emptied slowly Tuesday morning. A few residents who had attended the workshop lingered near the back, flipping through the printed budget documents left on a side table. One man, who declined to give his name, shook his head as he scanned the numbers.

"Twelve million dollars," he said. "And hurricane season just started."

articles.label: Development
articles.headline: The Bluffs project breaks ground next week. Here's what 15 years of delays actually cost Pensacola.
articles.dek: A timeline of false starts, withdrawn investors, and shifting city priorities behind the waterfront development that was supposed to transform downtown.
brief: The Bluffs waterfront development breaks ground June 11 after 15 years of failed attempts, withdrawn investors, and three separate city administrations
Original 2011 projections estimated $47 million in tax revenue over 20 years; adjusted for inflation and lost time, the delay cost the city an estimated $31 million in unrealized economic activity
The current $218 million project is roughly half the density of the 2015 proposal that collapsed when its primary investor pulled out amid fraud allegations
articles.body:
The dirt lot at the corner of Main Street and Bayfront Parkway has been empty so long that the hand-painted "Future Home Of" sign rotted off its posts. Someone replaced it with a piece of plywood spraypainted with a question mark. That was 2019. The plywood is still there.

Next Wednesday, crews will finally move earth on The Bluffs, a 4.2-acre mixed-use development that city officials have been promising since George W. Bush's second term. Mayor Sandra Chen will hold a ceremonial shovel. There will be renderings on easels. The Pensacola Chamber will send someone to say the word "transformational."

What no one will mention is what those 15 years actually cost.

The original vision

In 2011, the Pensacola City Council approved a development agreement with Emerald Coast Partners for a project then called Bayview Landing. The proposal included a 180-room hotel, 240 residential units, ground-floor retail and a public plaza connecting downtown to the waterfront.

City projections at the time estimated the development would generate $47 million in property tax revenue over 20 years and create 850 permanent jobs. The developer requested $8.2 million in tax increment financing. Council approved it 6-1.

"This is the most significant investment in downtown Pensacola in a generation," then-Mayor Mike Wiggins said at the signing ceremony.

Emerald Coast Partners broke ground in March 2012. They poured a foundation. Then they stopped.

The first collapse

By August 2012, Emerald Coast Partners had missed three construction benchmarks. Internal emails obtained through public records requests show city staff growing increasingly alarmed. "They're not returning calls," Community Redevelopment Agency director Tom Hendricks wrote to the city attorney. "Something is wrong."

Something was. The firm's principal investor, a Miami-based real estate fund, had pulled its $40 million commitment after disputes over cost overruns. Emerald Coast Partners tried to find replacement financing for 14 months. In October 2013, they formally withdrew from the agreement.

The city was left with a half-poured foundation and a $1.2 million hole in the CRA budget where anticipated tax revenue was supposed to be.

The Ardmore years

In 2015, a Birmingham developer called Ardmore Capital submitted an unsolicited proposal for the same site. Their vision was bigger: 320 residential units, a 220-room boutique hotel, a food hall and a rooftop bar. Total investment: $185 million.

Ardmore's principal, David Chen (no relation to the current mayor), had developed similar projects in Nashville and Charlotte. His pitch to council emphasized "new urbanism" and "18-hour neighborhoods." Council members were enthusiastic. The CRA was desperate.

The city approved a new development agreement in February 2016, this time with more stringent performance benchmarks and a $12 million TIF package. Ardmore began demolition of the old Emerald Coast foundation in April.

Then the SEC filed fraud charges against David Chen's brother, who ran a related investment fund. The charges were unrelated to the Pensacola project, but they spooked Ardmore's institutional investors. By September 2016, the company had entered "strategic restructuring." By January 2017, they were gone.

The wilderness period

Between 2017 and 2022, the city entertained at least seven proposals for the site. None advanced past initial discussions.

Part of the problem was reputation. "Developers talk to each other," said Marcus Webb, a commercial real estate broker who represented two of the failed bidders. "The site had a history. People thought it was cursed."

Part of the problem was the city. Three different CRA directors cycled through during this period. Each had different priorities. Council turnover meant institutional knowledge disappeared. Files were lost. Relationships had to be rebuilt from scratch.

"There was no continuity," said former Councilwoman Diane Mack, who served from 2014 to 2020. "Every time we got close, something would change internally and we'd have to start over."

The lot sat empty. Weeds grew through the gravel. In 2020, someone dumped a refrigerator there. It took the city three weeks to remove it.

What the delay cost

Calculating the true cost of 15 years of inaction requires some assumptions. But the basic math is straightforward.

The original 2011 projections estimated $2.35 million per year in property tax revenue once the development stabilized. Adjusted for inflation, that's roughly $3.1 million in 2026 dollars. If the project had been completed on its original 2014 timeline, the city would have collected approximately 12 years of that revenue by now.

That's $37 million in property taxes alone. Add foregone sales tax from retail and hospitality, and the number approaches $45 million.

Then there are the direct costs. The city spent $2.8 million on environmental remediation, site preparation and legal fees across the three failed development attempts. Staff time is harder to quantify but not trivial: hundreds of hours of negotiations, council meetings and public hearings that produced nothing.

The Escambia County Property Appraiser's office currently values the vacant lot at $4.2 million. A completed development of the originally planned density would be assessed at roughly $85 million. Every year the lot sat empty, the county and city lost the tax differential.

"Opportunity cost is real even when you can't see it," said Dr. Angela Torres, an economist at the University of West Florida who studies regional development. "That money would have circulated through the local economy. It would have supported other businesses, other jobs. The ripple effects compound."

The current project

The Bluffs, as currently approved, is more modest than either previous proposal. The development includes 180 residential units (60 fewer than Ardmore planned), a 140-room hotel, 22,000 square feet of retail and restaurant space and a half-acre public plaza.

The developer, Atlanta-based Southfield Communities, has completed similar projects in Savannah and St. Petersburg. Their financing is secured through a consortium of regional banks. The city's TIF contribution is $9.4 million spread over 15 years.

Construction is expected to take 26 months. If the timeline holds, the first residents would move in by late 2028.

"We're not trying to reinvent anything," Southfield vice president Karen Okonkwo said at the March council meeting where the final agreement was approved. "We're trying to build something that works, that's financeable, that will actually get done."

She did not mention the previous failures. No one on council asked about them.

What remains

The plywood sign with the question mark is still there as of this week. A city spokesperson said it will be removed before the groundbreaking ceremony.

Tom Hendricks, the former CRA director who watched the first deal collapse, retired in 2019. Reached by phone, he declined to comment on the record but said he planned to attend the groundbreaking.

"I just want to see a shovel in the ground," he said. "That's all. Just a shovel in the ground."

Diane Mack, the former councilwoman, was less sanguine. "We're celebrating something that should have happened when my kids were in elementary school," she said. "They're in college now. That's what 15 years means. That's what it actually looks like."

The ceremony begins at 10 a.m. Wednesday. Parking will be available in the lot across Bayfront Parkway, the one the city considered developing in 2018 before that proposal, too, fell apart.

articles.label: NAS Pensacola
articles.headline: Blue Angels homecoming week brings 200,000 visitors. The city still hasn't fixed the traffic plan.
articles.dek: Last year's gridlock left beachgoers stranded for hours. Officials say they're ready this time. The numbers suggest otherwise.
brief: Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show expects 200,000 attendees over two days at NAS Pensacola
2025 event left thousands stranded in 4-hour traffic backups on Barrancas Avenue and Navy Boulevard
City's updated traffic plan adds only one additional traffic control point despite 15% attendance increase
articles.body:
The line of brake lights stretched from the NAS Pensacola main gate to I-110. It was 2:47 p.m. on a Saturday last July, and Maria Delgado had been sitting in her Honda Civic for two hours and twelve minutes. Her two kids had already gone through the snacks. The AC was straining. The show had ended ninety minutes earlier.

"We could see the planes from the car," Delgado said. "That was the only part of the air show we actually saw."

She wasn't alone. Last year's Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show drew an estimated 175,000 visitors over two days. Thousands of them spent more time in traffic than watching the demonstration team fly. Social media filled with photos of gridlocked Navy Boulevard. Local tow companies reported their busiest weekend of the year—overheated engines, empty gas tanks, a few fender benders from frustrated drivers trying to cut through the Warrington neighborhood.

Now the 2026 Homecoming is ten days away. Organizers expect 200,000 attendees. The Pensacola Police Department released its updated traffic management plan last week.

It adds one additional traffic control officer.

The bottleneck that won't budge

The problem is geography. NAS Pensacola sits on a peninsula. Three roads in, three roads out: Navy Boulevard, Barrancas Avenue, and Blue Angel Parkway. During normal operations, this works fine. During an air show that quintuples the base population in a single morning, it does not.

"You're funneling 80,000 people through infrastructure designed for maybe 15,000," said Dr. Rebecca Tran, a transportation engineer at the University of West Florida who has studied Pensacola's special event traffic patterns. "There's no engineering solution that fixes that. You need demand management."

Demand management means spreading arrivals and departures across longer windows. It means incentivizing alternative transportation. It means, possibly, capping attendance.

The Navy and the city have tried some of this. Free shuttle service from Pensacola Beach and downtown started in 2019. A park-and-ride lot at Pensacola State College opened in 2023. Reserved parking with staggered departure times was piloted last year.

The shuttles moved about 3,000 people per day in 2025. The park-and-ride served another 2,500. That left roughly 85% of attendees arriving in personal vehicles.

What the city says

Pensacola Police Chief Marcus Webb addressed the traffic plan at a City Council meeting on May 28. He acknowledged last year's problems.

"We had a perfect storm situation," Webb said. "Higher than expected attendance, an accident on Navy Boulevard that blocked a lane for forty minutes, and some confusion at the checkpoint that slowed processing."

The 2026 plan, Webb said, includes better communication between traffic control points, a dedicated tow truck stationed at the I-110 interchange, and the additional officer at the Barrancas Avenue gate. The department is also coordinating with Escambia County Sheriff's Office for overflow support "if needed."

Council member Jared Patterson asked about expanding shuttle capacity.

"That's really a Navy decision," Webb said. "We support whatever they want to do there."

The Navy's public affairs office did not respond to questions about shuttle capacity or potential attendance limits. A spokesperson confirmed the air show schedule and directed further questions to the Pensacola base commanding officer, who was unavailable.

The numbers problem

Here is what the traffic plan does not address: the math.

Navy Boulevard has a peak capacity of roughly 1,800 vehicles per hour under normal conditions. With security checkpoints active, that drops to approximately 900. At an average of 2.3 occupants per vehicle, that's 2,070 people per hour.

The air show runs from 10 a.m. to 4 p.m. Gates open at 8 a.m. If every arriving vehicle came between 8 a.m. and noon—an optimistic spread—Navy Boulevard alone could theoretically process 36,000 people. Barrancas Avenue and Blue Angel Parkway add capacity, but with the same checkpoint constraints.

Maximum theoretical throughput across all three entrances: roughly 80,000 people in a four-hour arrival window.

Expected single-day attendance: 100,000.

"The only way it works is if people come very early or accept they'll miss the start," Tran said. "And nobody plans to miss the start."

The departure math is worse. The show ends at 4 p.m. Everyone leaves at once. There is no staggering incentive that overcomes the universal human desire to beat traffic by leaving immediately.

What other cities do

The Miramar Air Show in San Diego faces similar constraints—a military base on a peninsula, limited road access. In 2024, organizers implemented mandatory shuttle service for general admission. Personal vehicles were restricted to VIP parking pass holders. Attendance was capped at 125,000 per day.

Traffic complaints dropped 60% from the previous year, according to Miramar's after-action report.

The EAA AirVenture show in Oshkosh, Wisconsin—the largest air show in the country—uses a completely different model. Attendees camp on the airfield. Many fly in. A dedicated highway off-ramp opens only during the event.

Pensacola has none of these advantages. No dedicated infrastructure. No mandatory transit requirement. No attendance cap. What it has is a willing audience and a hope that this year will be different.

The cost of doing nothing

Lost in the traffic discussion is what gridlock actually costs.

Local businesses along the arrival corridors report a split effect. Gas stations and fast food restaurants see a bump. But the Warrington and Barrancas neighborhoods become effectively impassable for residents. Small businesses without air show traffic see customers stay away entirely.

"People know it's air show weekend," said Denise Watkins, who owns a hair salon on Navy Boulevard. "My regulars reschedule. I basically lose two days of business so other people can sit in traffic outside my window."

Emergency response is the larger concern. Last year, a medical call in Warrington took eleven minutes longer than average to reach because the responding ambulance couldn't navigate the backed-up streets. The patient—a 67-year-old man with chest pain—survived. The incident appeared in the fire department's after-action review as a "notable concern."

Fire Chief William Odom said the department pre-positions additional units in the affected area during the air show. "We plan for it," he said. "But there's no way to fully mitigate the access issues."

Ten days out

The Blue Angels will fly. The crowd will come. The traffic will build.

NAS Pensacola's website encourages attendees to arrive early, use the shuttle service, and bring patience. The Pensacola Police Department's traffic advisory recommends allowing "extra travel time" and following the directions of traffic control officers.

Maria Delgado said she's not going back.

"We tried," she said. "My kids were so excited. But sitting in a hot car for four hours with two children—that's not a family memory I want to make again."

She said they'll watch from Pensacola Beach this year. The view isn't as good. But the parking is free and the exit is easy.

The Blue Angels Homecoming Air Show runs Saturday, June 13 and Sunday, June 14. Gates open at 8 a.m. The demonstration begins at 2 p.m. both days.
